an1.51:1.1: “Radiant” (_pabhassara_) describes the mind in absorption ([mn140:20.3](), [sn46.33:2.1](), [an3.102:1.6](), [an5.23:2.5]()). It is one of many terms depicting meditative immersion as bright, luminous, clear, etc. But it has the special sense of light that “shines forth” when freed from obstacles. See too [dn1:2.2.2](), [dn11:85.19](), [thag20.1:59.6](), [an3.101:1.11](), [ja534:23.2](), and notes there. Etymologically, the Sanskrit form _prabhāsvara_ shows that it should be traced to _pabhā(s)_ + _vara_ in the sense “sublime radiance”. Related forms are typically used in elevated contexts such as gods or jhānas, although they have also come to be used for radiance in general, as that of a fire.
an1.51:1.4: [mn36]() details how the Buddha practiced “development of the mind” through the four absorptions to realize awakening. The topic is further discussed in relation to radiance and corruption in [mn127]().
an1.52:1.3: The Pali expression I translate as “truly” is _yathābhūta_, literally “as it has come to be”, or more loosely “in accordance with conditionality”. What has “come to be” is that which is produced according to the principles of dependent origination ([sn12.31:7.1]()), especially consciousness ([mn38:9.1]()).
an1.52:1.4: It is not the case that only enlightened beings can practice absorption. Rather, taken in context, the sense is that only an enlightened being truly understands the nature of absorption, namely, as a conditioned state of mind rather than an eternal metaphysical entity.
an1.56:1.1: This Sutta and the next express in prose ideas better known from the famous verses that open the Dhammapada ([dhp1]()–2); see there for further notes. Taking prose and verse together allows us to spell out the sequence: first intention, then actions, then consequences. Here, “intention” is _mano_, which, while often meaning simply “mind”, specially emphasizes the active role of the kammic mind, which is clearly the case here. The “actions” are mentioned in the Dhammapada as “one speaks or acts”. | For _pubbaṅgama_ as “leader’ of a group, see [sn45.1:2.1]() and note.
an1.56:1.2: This line shows that _dhammā_ includes the intention itself, as well as the actions it prompts, while the Dhammapada also mentions the consequences of happiness or suffering. It seems, then, that _dhammā_ includes intention, actions, and consequences, so I translate as generically as possible with “things”.
an1.58:1.1: Here begins a new series of discourses, which are the first to actually mention the number “one” and hence naturally belong to the Book of the Ones, rather than being artificially created by splitting longer discourses. Nonetheless, even here the “single things” are grouped in contrasting pairs. The fact that [an1.61]() and [an1.71]() both break their pairs across chapter boundaries suggests once more that _vagga_ divisions were imposed on a pre-existing text.
